extracted.subtask_description: Survey of national and international policies, laws, platform actions, fact‑checking initiatives, and educational responses to 'fake news' and disinformation across many countries. Includes examples, controversies, and implementation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary code of practice on disinformation (European Commission)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2018 the European Commission introduced a first voluntary code of practice on disinformation. In 2022 this will become a strengthen co-regulation scheme, with responsibility shared between the regulators and companies signatory to the code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended as a voluntary (to co-regulatory) mechanism for platforms and companies to commit to measures countering disinformation; it is meant to complement binding rules such as the Digital Services Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital Services Act provisions on combating disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Digital Services Act agreed by the 27-country European Union already includes a section on combating disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts as a legislative backbone which the voluntary/co-regulatory code complements; signals EU-level regulatory obligations for platforms regarding disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of international/multinational centres to combat disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials from 11 countries met in Helsinki in November 2016 and planned the formation of a center to combat disinformation cyber-warfare, combining efforts from multiple countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes multinational cooperation and shared resources to counter cross-border disinformation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government monitoring and hiring of specialists to counter propaganda (Sweden example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency identified fake news reports targeting Sweden and planned to hire additional security officials to fight back against campaigns of fraudulent information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State agencies may monitor information environments and allocate personnel/resources to detection and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform enforcement: account removal and takedowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as Facebook deleting 30,000 Facebook accounts in France associated with fake political information illustrate platforms removing accounts as an enforcement tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-level takedowns and suspensions are a primary mitigation method, but rely on platforms' policies and detection capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent fact-checking initiatives and civic debunking (e.g., StopFake, Aos Fatos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grassroots and independent projects (StopFake in Ukraine; Aos Fatos in Brazil) have been started to debunk fake news and provide corrective information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil-society and newsroom-led fact-checking is a non‑coercive remedy that seeks to correct the record and hold sources accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-run fact-checking and debunking sites (e.g., Singapore's Factually)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ministry of Communications and Information in Singapore set up Factually, a website intended to debunk false rumors regarding issues of public interest such as the environment, housing and transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official fact-check portals provide authoritative rebuttals but can raise concerns about government influence over information depending on legal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization and penal sanctions for dissemination of false information (Malta Article 82)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 82 of Malta's Criminal Code targets the malicious dissemination of fake news: anyone who deliberately spreads false information likely to alarm the public, disturb public order, or create commotion can be sentenced to imprisonment for one to three months; if resulting in a disturbance, imprisonment increases to one to six months and possible fine up to €1,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of criminal penalties aimed at discouraging malicious spread of false information; raises questions about proportionality and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties and broad anti-fake-news laws (Malaysia Anti-Fake News Bill 2018)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaysia's Anti-Fake News Bill 2018 deemed publishing and circulating misleading information a crime punishable by up to six years in prison and/or fines up to 500,000 ringgit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad criminalization can be politically contentious; critics warn vagueness risks persecuting satirists, opinion writers, and journalists who make errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduated legal response to falsehoods (Singapore POFMA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Bill (POFMA) allows authorities to respond through a graduated process: enforcing links to fact-checking statements, censorship of websites or assets on social media platforms, and criminal charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to provide a stepped toolkit (labels/corrections, takedowns, prosecutions); criticized for potential government self-censorship and increased control over social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency powers to remove/close websites with no appeal (Romania COVID-19 decree)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romania's emergency decree during COVID-19 gave authorities power to remove, report or close websites spreading 'fake news' about the pandemic, with no opportunity to appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how emergency contexts can enable rapid content removal but may remove due process and appeal protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic registration and disciplinary obligations to ensure truthful reporting (Italy Ordine Dei Giornalisti)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must be registered with the Ordine Dei Giornalisti (ODG) and respect its disciplinary and training obligations, to guarantee 'correct and truthful information, intended as right of individuals and of the community'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional regulation and discipline are used in some jurisdictions to promote accuracy and accountability among journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to report fake news to law enforcement portals (Italy Polizia di Stato)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2018 it is possible to report fake news directly on the Polizia di Stato website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a mechanism for citizens to alert authorities, linking public reporting to potential enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public 'blacklists' or 'hall of shame' listings and due-process concerns (EU East StratCom case)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EU's East StratCom Task Force compiled a 'hall of shame' list of articles with suspected Kremlin attempts to influence political decisions; controversy arose when outlets claimed they had been wrongfully singled out with no forewarning or opportunity to appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public naming can expose suspected disinformation but risks wrongful identification and free‑press implications; due process and appeals are governance concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared technical identifiers as investigative signals (shared AdSense/Analytics IDs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Philippine-audience fake news websites appeared to be controlled by the same operators as they share common Google AdSense and Google Analytics IDs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators can use technical footprints (ad/analytics IDs) to link networks of sites; useful for attribution and disruption of coordinated operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media literacy education to build critical thinking (Taiwan example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taiwan reformed policy to include 'media literacy' in school curriculum to develop critical-thinking skills needed while using social media and to analyze propaganda and sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term preventive measure focused on education to reduce susceptibility to disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology caution: use 'information disorder' rather than 'fake news' (Claire Wardle advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr Claire Wardle advised against using the term 'fake news' in some circumstances, saying the term is 'woefully inadequate' because much content used as examples is genuine but used out of context or manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends more precise framing (e.g., 'information disorder') to capture the variety of problematic content (misinformation, disinformation, malinformation) and avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of stylistic/branding mimicry by deceptive sites (El País observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fake sites 'have similar names, typography, layouts and are deliberately confusing' to mislead readers into believing they are mainstream outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying branding mimicry (names, layouts) is an anti-pattern detection method for spotting deceptive or impersonating sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and government tensions over responsibility and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook and Google opposed the proposed Singapore law, claiming existing legislation was adequate and that educating citizens is an effective way to distinguish reliable information; tensions exist between platform self-regulation and government mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy responses must balance platform responsibility, governmental oversight, and civil liberties; cooperation and contestation are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messaging apps as critical vectors for disinformation (WhatsApp examples: India, Colombia, Indonesia)
rubrics_metrics.description: WhatsApp has been a major vector for fake news in countries such as India and Colombia; in Indonesia misinformation on social media and messaging apps rose around elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions may include blocking URLs, fact-check apps, public briefings, and targeted education because messaging platforms present unique amplification and privacy/technical challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: State actors and official misinformation complicate attribution (examples from Ukraine and China)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances include the staged assassination claim in Ukraine delivered by officials, and the Chinese government accusing Western media of 'fake news' to justify censorship; states can be both targets and producers of misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When state actors are involved, responses are politically sensitive and may involve intelligence, diplomatic, and legal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of violence from misinformation in low‑connectivity/rapidly digitizing countries (Myanmar example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake stories shared online in Myanmar correlated with violence against Muslim communities; countries newer to Internet exposure can be particularly vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights need for rapid intervention, community-level education, and platform moderation tailored to contexts where misinformation can cause physical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom and investigative responses: dedicated fact-check positions
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations such as El País created fact‑checking positions and blogs (e.g., 'Hechos') specifically to respond to and debunk fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding fact-checking capacity within newsrooms is a proactive editorial standard to protect public information quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy and civil‑liberties concerns around anti‑disinformation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Several country examples (Malaysia, Singapore, China) show critics warn anti-fake-news statutes can be vague, used for political targeting, or to justify censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design should account for freedom of expression, proportionality, clarity of offences, and safeguards against misuse.
